title: Online Students
text:
1In Canvas, go to People → Groups and join a pod whose time you can make. Each pod holds up to 4 people.
  2Do the same before-class prep as everyone else, before your pod meets.
  3Run the activity with your pod on a video call at your pod's time.

title: Online Students
text:
Video-interview tips

Put your camera at eye level, and look at the camera when you’re making a key point.
Light your face from the front with a window or lamp. Avoid light coming from behind you.
Notes on a sticky note next to the camera are fine. Reading a script off the screen is noticeable.
Live calls: unmute, pause for a beat, then answer, because lag can make people talk over each other.

title: Climate Action Analyst
text:
Pitkin County · Aspen, CO (hybrid) · $73,080 – $127,890
Based on a real posting (view original, posted October 21, 2026 (closes November 11, 2026), accessed November 3, 2026). Postings close. Interview for it anyway.

title: Climate Action Analyst
text:
The role

Build the county’s Climate Action Plan goals into department policies, budgets, and day-to-day operations.
Research and recommend policy on transportation, building performance, renewable energy, waste, and adaptation.
Collect and track climate, energy, and emissions data, build tracking tools, and report progress to the Board of County Commissioners.
Find and manage grants, program budgets, and consultants.
Represent the county in regional climate partnerships, and lead the county’s long-term disaster recovery function when the emergency operations center is activated.

title: Climate Action Analyst
text:
What they’re looking for

About 3+ years of experience in climate policy, sustainability, energy, or environmental policy analysis.
A degree in environmental science, public policy, planning, or a related field.
Knowledge of GHG inventories, climate action planning, and adaptation.
Preferred: local-government, grant, and community-outreach experience.







Reality check: The posting asks for 3+ years of experience. Be ready to explain how your PSM internship, projects, and earlier jobs add up to that.

title: Climate Action Analyst
text:
Know the employer
Pitkin County covers Aspen and the upper Roaring Fork Valley. It’s a small county with a big tourism economy, high-emitting visitor travel and second homes, and direct exposure to wildfire, drought, and a shrinking snowpack.

title: Climate Action Analyst
text:
Interview room






Candidate: stop reading here. Everything below is for the panel.
Panelists: open only your own seat. Each seat’s questions were written for this job. Ask one of them, then follow up in your character’s style.



Every round, each panelist draws a mood card. Keep it secret and play it lightly.


  🎲 Draw a mood card
  Hide
  Tap to draw. Draw again each round.








NoteSeat A · Riley, the Technical Lead (click to open)





Here, you are: The county’s data and GIS manager, and its contact for the regional emissions inventory.
Ask one of these:

“Our emissions inventory is two years old and partly modeled. How would you track Climate Action Plan progress between inventories?”
“Visitor air travel and second homes are huge here. How would you decide what counts as ‘our’ emissions and what doesn’t?”

Then follow up: when they use a buzzword (modeled, analyzed, managed, data-driven), ask “What specifically did you do?” or “How would you know if that was wrong?”


More about Riley

Story. A data feed your team depends on broke again last week, and you’ve been patching it ever since. You’ve been burned by hires who listed “R” and “GIS” on their résumé and then couldn’t clean a messy spreadsheet.
Quirks. Friendly but literal. You ask for numbers (“How many sites? How many years?”) and take notes.
Listen for: specific tools and steps, real QA/QC habits, and honesty about gaps.










NoteSeat B · Pat, Search Committee Chair (click to open)





Here, you are: Assistant County Manager. You own the budget and the Commissioners’ agenda.
Ask one of these:

“The Commissioners want to know on Tuesday whether we’re on track with the Climate Action Plan. What goes on your one slide?”
“We have $50,000 in grant match and three departments that want it: buildings, transit, and wildfire mitigation. How would you recommend splitting it?”

Then follow up: politely interrupt idealistic answers with “That sounds great in a seminar. What’s the version we can deliver by Friday?” If an answer runs past about 90 seconds: “Give me the headline.”


More about Pat

Story. You chair this search committee. Your puppy chewed up a corner of the carpet overnight, so the morning started early, and you have a budget meeting right after this. You love good science that ships on time.
Quirks. You keep an eye on the clock.
Listen for: prioritization, concrete deliverables, and concise answers.










NoteSeat C · Morgan, the Team & Mission Lead (click to open)





Here, you are: The county’s community engagement lead.
Ask one of these:

“Much of the valley’s workforce commutes in from downvalley because they can’t afford to live here. How does that change how you talk about transportation emissions?”
“This role also leads long-term recovery after a disaster. Tell me about a time you had to work in a chaotic, high-stakes situation.”

Then follow up: “What would the other person say happened?” or “What did that teach you about how you work?” After each answer, pause for a few seconds before speaking.


More about Morgan

Story. Last week you ran a field day for a group of ninth-graders, and it reminded you how hard it is to explain this work simply. You’ve seen strong scientists struggle because they couldn’t explain their work to a non-scientist or get along with the person at the next desk.
Quirks. Warm, and comfortable with silence.
Listen for: a real story (STAR), empathy, self-awareness, and plain language.










NoteSeat D · Dale, the Outside Stakeholder (pods of 5) (click to open)





Here, you are: Owner of a small lodge in Aspen who sits on a county citizen advisory board.
Ask one of these:

“The building-performance rules you’d be pushing could cost me six figures to retrofit my lodge. Why should I support them?”
“Every few years the county announces a new climate plan. What’s different this time?”

Then follow up: say “Huh?” every time they use an acronym or jargon without explaining it.


More about Dale

Story. You’re not on staff. You drove a couple of hours to sit in on this panel because this hire will be working with you.
Quirks. Plainspoken and skeptical, but not hostile. If they actually listen, you warm up.
Listen for: plain language, respect, and whether they ask you questions.










NoteSeat A+B · Riley-Pat, the Hiring Manager (pods of 3) (click to open)





Pods of 3 only. You’re both Riley and Pat. Ask one Seat A question and one Seat B question from this job, and use both follow-ups: “What specifically did you do?” and “What’s the version we can deliver by Friday?”

title: Sustainability Analyst
text:
Johns Manville · Littleton or Denver, CO (hybrid, ~20% travel) · $62,800 – $86,400 + bonus
Based on a real posting (view original, posted October 13, 2026, accessed November 3, 2026). Postings close. Interview for it anyway.

title: Sustainability Analyst
text:
The role

Own and improve the company’s annual Scope 1, 2, and 3 greenhouse gas inventory, from collecting energy, logistics, and supplier data through validating it.
Run life cycle assessments (cradle-to-gate and full LCA) and support Environmental Product Declarations for building products.
Build dashboards and turn the numbers into recommendations for plant, product, and leadership teams.
Support sustainability disclosures and ratings (CDP, EcoVadis) and customer data requests.
Work with cross-functional teams on energy, waste, and circularity projects.

title: Sustainability Analyst
text:
What they’re looking for

A degree in sustainability, environmental science, engineering, or a related field.
Working knowledge of the GHG Protocol and ISO 14064.
Hands-on LCA or product carbon footprint experience (SimaPro or GaBi is a plus).
Strong Excel skills, with Power BI a plus. Ability to explain technical results to non-experts.
The posting encourages people to apply even if they don’t meet every listed requirement.

Johns Manville is a Denver-headquartered building-products manufacturer (insulation, roofing, and engineered products) and a Berkshire Hathaway company. Architects and builders increasingly ask for product-level carbon data, which is a big reason this role exists.

The role

Build and maintain GIS data models and databases for the city’s drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater systems (“One Water”).
Write scripts to automate data capture, conversion, and quality checks.
Run spatial and statistical analyses, and produce operational and regulatory maps.
Configure and support GIS apps and servers used by field crews.

text:

Knowledge of coordinate systems, map projections, and federal geospatial data standards.
Strong written and verbal communication.

Fort Collins Utilities is a city-owned utility. Its “One Water” approach manages drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater as a single system, which makes good integrated spatial data especially valuable.

title: Water Resources Engineer or Hydrologist
text:
BBA Water Consultants · Englewood, CO (Salida branch office) · $65,000 – $105,000
Based on a real posting (view original, posted September 2026 (open until filled), accessed November 3, 2026). Postings close. Interview for it anyway.

title: Water Resources Engineer or Hydrologist
text:
The role

Support clients such as municipalities, water districts, and private owners with day-to-day water operations and water supply planning.
Provide technical support for Colorado Water Court cases.
Explain technical water concepts clearly to clients, attorneys, and the court.
Do analyses like historical consumptive use and water rights administration work.

title: Water Resources Engineer or Hydrologist
text:
What they’re looking for

A BS and/or MS in engineering, hydrology, or water resources, with 0–5 years of Colorado water resources experience.
Strong writing, speaking, and time management skills, and strong Excel skills.
Pluses: programming, GIS, and familiarity with Colorado water law and water rights administration.
Hydrologists are expected to hold or work toward Professional Hydrologist (PH) certification. Engineers are expected to hold or work toward PE licensure.







Reality check: If you haven’t taken Water Law for Non-Lawyers or something similar, brush up on prior appropriation, and be ready to explain how you’d work toward PH certification.

BBA Water Consultants is a Denver-area firm focused on Colorado water rights, water supply, and Water Court work. Colorado’s prior-appropriation system makes this kind of consulting a large niche, and much of it involves converting water from agricultural to municipal use.

title: Mock Interview Panel
text:
Before class
About 30–45 minutes.

Pick a job on the Job Board, plus a backup. It’s fine if a podmate picks the same one.
Read the real posting (linked on each job page). Find their top 3 must-haves, and jot down a real example of yours for each.
Practice a 60-second pitch out loud. Use the toolkit below.
Write one question you’d genuinely want to ask the panel.
Bring a charged device.







On your own job’s page, stop at “Know the employer.” The Interview room below that is for the panel. Not knowing the questions is part of the practice.

title: Mock Interview Panel
text:
In class
Each round takes 10 minutes, and the Timer keeps every pod in step.







Time
What happens




1 min · Set up
The candidate names their job. Panelists open that job’s page, scroll to the Interview room, open their own seat, and draw a mood card.


1 min · Pitch
The candidate gives their 60-second pitch. The panel listens.


5 min · Questions
Each panelist, in seat order, asks one question in character and follows up.


1 min · Your question
The candidate asks the panel their question.


2 min · Debrief
Everyone drops character. Each panelist gives three one-line notes (below).



Then rotate to the next person.

title: Mock Interview Panel
text:
Debrief: three one-liners
When the debrief starts, drop character. Each panelist says:

Hired-peer moment: when they sounded like a colleague you’d want.
Hedge moment: when they rambled, hedged, or sounded like a seminar.
One thing to try next time.

Be specific (“When you walked through cleaning the streamflow data, I believed you”) rather than general (“Good job!”).

title: Mock Interview Panel
text:
Candidate toolkit






Note60-second pitch formula






“I’m [name], and I [your focus]. Most recently I [one concrete thing you built, analyzed, or managed]. I’m interested in [this role] at [this employer] because [something specific from the posting]. I’d bring [the one or two skills they need most].”










NoteSTAR for “Tell me about a time…”






Situation: one or two sentences of context.
Task: what you were responsible for.
Action: what you did. Spend most of your time here, and say “I,” not “we.”
Result: what happened (with a number if you have one) and what you learned.










NoteWhen you don’t know something






“I haven’t used [X] directly. The closest thing I’ve done is [Y], where I [specific]. Here’s how I’d get up to speed on [X]…”

This beats bluffing every time.

title: Mock Interview Panel
text:
Ground rules

Tough but fair. The point is realistic practice, not “winning.”
No illegal questions, even in character: nothing about age, family, pregnancy, religion, national origin, or disability.
Stumbling is the point. Better to freeze here than in a real interview.

Matthew R.V. Ross (Department of Ecosystem Science and Sustainability, Colorado State University) created this site for students in the Professional Science Master’s in Ecosystem Science and Sustainability. Matthew designed the activity’s goals and constraints, directed every revision, and is responsible for the content.

title: About & AI Disclosure
text:
How AI was used

Concept: the first version of the activity (rotating pods, interviewer archetypes, a paperless setup) was brainstormed with Google Gemini.
Building the site: Claude Opus 5.5 (High effort) wrote the text on every page. That includes the instructions, the panel characters and mood cards, every interview question, and the online options. It also wrote the timer and mood-card code and the Quarto site configuration.
Job postings: Claude searched public job boards for real Colorado postings that match the program’s focus areas. It opened and checked each posting on the employer’s page or a public listing, then paraphrased the duties and qualifications. Each job page links to the original.
Revision: the instructor reviewed drafts and asked for specific changes, including tone, round timing, the online format, and questions tied to each job. Claude made those changes.

title: About & AI Disclosure
text:
About the job postings

Each job is based on a real public posting, accessed November 3, 2026. Summaries are paraphrased. The original posting is the authoritative source.
Postings close. A closed posting is still realistic practice.
The employers named here are not affiliated with this activity and have not reviewed or endorsed it.
The panel characters (Riley, Pat, Morgan, Dale), their “Here, you are” roles, and every interview question are fictional. They were written for practice and don’t describe real people at these organizations.

title: EPS I – SWAP Data/Program Coordinator
text:
Colorado Dept. of Public Health & Environment · Denver, CO (10–15% statewide travel) · $66,400 – $79,680
Based on a real posting (view original, posted November 3, 2026 (closes November 17, 2026), accessed November 3, 2026). Postings close. Interview for it anyway.

title: EPS I – SWAP Data/Program Coordinator
text:
The role

Coordinate Colorado’s Source Water Assessment and Protection (SWAP) program, which helps communities protect the source waters behind their drinking-water supplies.
Do outreach, training, and technical support for public water systems, local health departments, and grant recipients.
Manage grant tracking, contracting, and reporting, including work tied to new PFAS requirements.
Maintain the SWAP database and maps, and respond to data and GIS requests.
Write program materials, procedures, and web content.

title: EPS I – SWAP Data/Program Coordinator
text:
What they’re looking for

Minimum: a bachelor’s in environmental science, natural resources, hydrology, or a related field, plus 1 year of experience managing water-quality projects.
Preferred: a master’s degree.
Preferred: watershed or source-water project experience, plus mapping, data analysis, and reporting skills (ArcGIS, spreadsheets).
Preferred: familiarity with the Safe Drinking Water Act or the Colorado Water Quality Control Act, and experience working across agencies and communities.
The position is open to Colorado residents only.

title: EPS I – SWAP Data/Program Coordinator
text:
Know the employer
CDPHE’s Water Quality Control Division regulates drinking water and water quality statewide. The SWAP program is voluntary and partnership-based, so much of the job is persuading people rather than enforcing rules.

Interview room






Candidate: stop reading here. Everything below is for the panel.
Panelists: open only your own seat. Each seat’s questions were written for this job. Ask one of them, then follow up in your character’s style.



Every round, each panelist draws a mood card. Keep it secret and play it lightly.


  🎲 Draw a mood card
  Hide
  Tap to draw. Draw again each round.








NoteSeat A · Riley, the Technical Lead (click to open)





Here, you are: The unit’s GIS and data lead. You inherited the SWAP database and its decades of inconsistent records.
Ask one of these:

“A legislator’s office wants a map of every source water protection area by Friday. Our database has records entered by many different people over decades. What do you check before you send it?”
“How would you prioritize which source water areas are most at risk from PFAS? What data would you combine?”

Then follow up: when they use a buzzword (modeled, analyzed, managed, data-driven), ask “What specifically did you do?” or “How would you know if that was wrong?”


More about Riley

Story. A data feed your team depends on broke again last week, and you’ve been patching it ever since. You’ve been burned by hires who listed “R” and “GIS” on their résumé and then couldn’t clean a messy spreadsheet.
Quirks. Friendly but literal. You ask for numbers (“How many sites? How many years?”) and take notes.
Listen for: specific tools and steps, real QA/QC habits, and honesty about gaps.










NoteSeat B · Pat, Search Committee Chair (click to open)





Here, you are: Unit Manager. You own the grant budget and the federal reporting deadlines.
Ask one of these:

“We have grant money for about 15 communities and 40 are interested. How do you decide who gets it, and how do you tell the rest?”
“Federal reporting, two grant deadlines, and a statewide training workshop all land in the same month. How do you plan it?”

Then follow up: politely interrupt idealistic answers with “That sounds great in a seminar. What’s the version we can deliver by Friday?” If an answer runs past about 90 seconds: “Give me the headline.”


More about Pat

Story. You chair this search committee. Your puppy chewed up a corner of the carpet overnight, so the morning started early, and you have a budget meeting right after this. You love good science that ships on time.
Quirks. You keep an eye on the clock.
Listen for: prioritization, concrete deliverables, and concise answers.










NoteSeat C · Morgan, the Team & Mission Lead (click to open)





Here, you are: Outreach lead who works with local health departments and small water systems.
Ask one of these:

“A small mountain town with one part-time water operator wants to join SWAP but says they don’t have time for a ‘plan.’ How do you get them started?”
“Explain what ‘source water protection’ means to me like I’m a town council member who’s never heard the term.”

Then follow up: “What would the other person say happened?” or “What did that teach you about how you work?” After each answer, pause for a few seconds before speaking.


More about Morgan

Story. Last week you ran a field day for a group of ninth-graders, and it reminded you how hard it is to explain this work simply. You’ve seen strong scientists struggle because they couldn’t explain their work to a non-scientist or get along with the person at the next desk.
Quirks. Warm, and comfortable with silence.
Listen for: a real story (STAR), empathy, self-awareness, and plain language.










NoteSeat D · Dale, the Outside Stakeholder (pods of 5) (click to open)





Here, you are: The only operator of a small-town water system, who also plows the roads in winter.
Ask one of these:

“I’m the only operator here. What exactly do you need from me, and how long will it take?”
“The state keeps adding rules. Is this program going to turn into another regulation we have to pay for?”

Then follow up: say “Huh?” every time they use an acronym or jargon without explaining it.


More about Dale

Story. You’re not on staff. You drove a couple of hours to sit in on this panel because this hire will be working with you.
Quirks. Plainspoken and skeptical, but not hostile. If they actually listen, you warm up.
Listen for: plain language, respect, and whether they ask you questions.










NoteSeat A+B · Riley-Pat, the Hiring Manager (pods of 3) (click to open)





Pods of 3 only. You’re both Riley and Pat. Ask one Seat A question and one Seat B question from this job, and use both follow-ups: “What specifically did you do?” and “What’s the version we can deliver by Friday?”

text:
The role

Do technical, economic, and financial analysis for clients, including data collection and modeling.
Work on corporate GHG accounting, climate risk, ESG disclosure, and emissions-reduction (abatement) analysis.
Evaluate energy efficiency and renewable energy options.
Research market trends and help shape client sustainability strategies.
Help manage multi-client projects and write and present client-ready reports.

Willingness to travel a lot (the posting says up to 75% or more).

title: Agriculture Project Manager
text:
The role

Launch and run a new agricultural conservation program from concept to completion, including scopes, timelines, and budgets.
Give producers technical help on soil health, agronomy, grazing, irrigation, and water management.
Coordinate with NRCS, CSU Extension, FSA, local governments, and conservation nonprofits.
Write and manage grants and cost-share agreements, including reporting and reimbursements.
Prepare conservation plans and reports, and represent the district at community events.

title: Agriculture Project Manager
text:
What they’re looking for

A degree in agronomy, soil science, rangeland ecology, environmental science, or a related field.
About 3 years of agricultural or conservation experience, including familiarity with NRCS Farm Bill programs.
GIS and GPS skills.
Ability to lead projects independently and work directly with producers.
Preferred: grant writing and coordinating multiple partners.







Reality check: This one is a stretch if you haven’t worked with farm programs. If you pick it, be ready to talk about how you’d earn producers’ trust.

Rio Grande Water Conservation District · Alamosa, CO (onsite, heavy fieldwork) · From $28.85/hr (~$60,000), non-exempt
Based on a real posting (view original, posted October 2026 (applications due November 20, 2026), accessed November 3, 2026; more at rgwcd.org). Postings close. Interview for it anyway.

title: Groundwater Monitoring & Field Operations Lead
text:
The role

Lead the district’s monthly groundwater-level monitoring program across the San Luis Valley.
Verify, analyze, and report data in coordination with the USGS and the Colorado Division of Water Resources, and investigate odd readings.
Plan and coordinate field projects with staff, contractors, and landowners.
Oversee installation and maintenance of monitoring wells, and calibrate field instruments.
Keep detailed field logs and maintain equipment and vehicles.

title: Groundwater Monitoring & Field Operations Lead
text:
What they’re looking for

A bachelor’s degree in hydrology, natural resources, environmental science, or a related field, or equivalent experience.
Field data collection experience, plus GPS, GIS, and mobile data tools.
Preferred: 2+ years of hydrologic fieldwork, groundwater monitoring, and well installation experience.
Preferred: familiarity with Colorado groundwater management.
Ability to work independently outdoors in all weather.

title: Groundwater Monitoring & Field Operations Lead
text:
Know the employer
The Rio Grande Water Conservation District works on groundwater sustainability in the San Luis Valley. There, decades of irrigated agriculture and drought have drawn down the aquifers, and farmers formed groundwater sub-districts to bring them back into balance.

Listen for: a real story (STAR), empathy, self-awareness, and plain language.










NoteSeat D · Dale, the Outside Stakeholder (pods of 5)





Wants to know: Will this person waste my time, talk down to me, or actually help? Dale is a different person on every job, such as a supplier, a farmer, or a council member. The job page says who.
Then follow up: say “Huh?” every time they use an acronym or jargon without explaining it.


More about Dale

Story. You’re not on staff. You drove a couple of hours to sit in on this panel because this hire will be working with you.
Quirks. Plainspoken and skeptical, but not hostile. If they actually listen, you warm up.
Listen for: plain language, respect, and whether they ask you questions.










NoteSeat A+B · Riley-Pat, the Hiring Manager (pods of 3)





Pods of 3 only. You’re both Riley and Pat. Ask one Seat A question and one Seat B question from this job, and use both follow-ups: “What specifically did you do?” and “What’s the version we can deliver by Friday?”

title: Meet the Panel
text:
Ground rules for panelists

Details add realism; they’re not an attack. Stay tough but fair, and drop the act completely for the debrief.
No illegal questions, even in character: nothing about age, family status, pregnancy, religion, national origin, disability, or similar topics.
Keep the details about your character’s day, never about the candidate.
Off-script is fine. If the candidate says something interesting, follow it. Your seat’s questions are a starting point, not a script.
